nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What unique opportunity does the global scope of this analysis provide?
nodes.answer: The global scope provides a unique opportunity to examine how socioeconomic factors operate across diverse cultural, political, and economic contexts.
nodes.paragraph: Addressing socioeconomic disparities is essential for understanding environmental behavior, particularly in regions with pronounced inequality. Economic disparities weaken collective engagement by reducing national identification and shared responsibility (Baland et al., 2018; Ignatow, 2005). They also exacerbate educational line- qualities, limiting access to knowledge necessary for sustainable practices (Zreik, 2023). Additionally, financial constraints in less developed countries hinder prioritization of envi- ronmental concerns, reflecting the challenge of balancing economic needs with sustainabil- ity ( arko lu & Kentmen- in, 2015; Zreik, 2023). This study leverages data from over 60 countries spanning developed and developing economies to explore how socioeconomic factors such as income, education, and employ - ment status influence environmental perceptions and pro-environmental behaviors. The global scope of this analysis provides a unique opportunity to examine how these factors operate across diverse cultural, political, and economic contexts. By examining a wide array of demographic groups, this research offers insights into how sustainability policies can be tailored to meet the needs of different populations and socioeconomic strata. Fur - thermore, the findings from this study contribute to a growing body of literature that seeks to understand the intersection of economic development and environmental sustainability, offering both theoretical insights and practical implications for policymakers.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What factors have exacerbated the influence of UPFs and intensive ASFs on food culture?
nodes.answer: Factors include colonialism, economic and cultural globalization, and contemporary forms of economic colonialism (neocolonialism).
nodes.paragraph: Furthermore, the outputs from intensive ani- mal agriculture often constitute major ingredients in many UPFs, suggesting mutual rein- forcement of these foods, including via ready meals, fast-food, and the use of dairy-based ingredients for confectionery, instant coffee drinks, infant formula, and ice cream (Neri et al. 2023). Moreover, reconstituted meat products, including industrially produced sau- sages, nuggets and some burgers, are categorised as UPFs (Monteiro et al. 2019). The proliferation of UPFs and intensive ASFs has had a substantial impact on tradi- tional dietary patterns, resulting in the loss of food cultures , propelled initially by coloni- alism and later exacerbated by economic and cultural globalisation, as well as more con- temporary forms of economic colonialism (neocolonialism) (Holt Gim nez and Shattuck 2011; Otero et al. 2015). It has also been argued that UPF and intensive ASF dominance in the food supply disconnects populations from their traditional diets, reduces culinary skills, and shifts dietary preferences towards UPFs and intensively produced ASFs (Olstad et al. 2023).

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why does conventional economics find it challenging to examine alternative currencies?
nodes.answer: Conventional economics struggles to measure the impacts of alternative currencies because it is based on theoretical and normative conceptions of money that do not account for their heterogeneity, characteristics, and local usefulness.
nodes.paragraph: Yet, most orthodox economists affix a neutrality to it, both from economic and social points of view. In that vein, money is approached from a functional and technical angle (Fare 2016) devoid of any political aspect. Fare and Ahmed (2018) note that conventional economics pays marginal attention to alternative currencies, i.e. curren- cies that are alternatives or complements to mainstream state fiat currencies and that have limited functions and circuits of circulation. Indeed, conventional economics struggles to measure the impacts of alternative currencies because it is based on theoretical and normative conceptions of money that do not allow it to understand their heterogeneity, their characteristics and their usefulness at the local level. Since the creation in 1934 of the WIR (an independent comple- mentary currency system in Switzerland) and the establish - ment of a local exchange trading system (in Vancouver, Canada, in 1983), the emergence of alternative currencies has accelerated from the end of the twentieth century (Blanc 2018). The continuous development of alternative curren- cies can be seen as an unprecedented phenomenon on the scale of the monetary history of industrial societies (Blanc 2018).

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How does material culture differ from traditional views of goods as commodities?
nodes.answer: Material culture differs from the traditional view of goods as commodities by emphasizing that goods carry meaning beyond their economic value, offering insights into societal values and cultural practices.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Gender equity|Cultural norms|Cultural impact on economic opportunities_qna_004
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: McCracken (1986) discusses the cultural meaning of consumer goods. How does culture influence consumer behaviour and the perception of products?
nodes.answer: Culture influences consumer behaviour and product perception, as discussed by McCracken (1986), by shaping values and societal norms.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Gender equity|Cultural norms|Cultural impact on economic opportunities_qna_005
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: Why is culture considered a significant factor in shaping fashion and clothing purchasing behaviour?
nodes.answer: Culture is viewed as a "mental map" that provides knowledge and guidelines for individual behaviour based on personal values, social foundations, and traditions. Different cultures can influence consumer attitudes and responses towards fashion stimuli.

nodes.question: How does value chain analysis impact our understanding of economic activities?
nodes.answer: It helps to understand the monetary and employment impacts at each stage of the activity, providing insight into the distribution of wealth generated.
nodes.paragraph: 2016, 2020). On the other hand, the enlargement of harbour-based fisheries economic analysis to a broader economic impact analysis has been done mainly through regional input out- put models (Garza-Gil et al. 2017; Garc a-de-la-Fuente et al. 2020; Raffray et al. 2022), computable general equilibrium models (Akbari et al. 2023), and value chain analyses (de la Puente and Christensen 2024). This latter type of analy - sis is used to understand how the wealth (and sometimes employment) generated by an economic activity is distrib- uted among the different stakeholders involved, from the beginning of the activity to its completion. In the case of fisheries, the aim is to better understand the impact, in mon- etary and employment terms, at each stage through which seafood moves from the boat to the plate, including catching, distribution, processing, and commercialization. Value chain has been widely used all over the world in very different contexts (Gudmundsson et al. 2006; Failler et al. 2014; FAO and Neven 2014; Khan and Chuenpagdee 2014; Pascual- Fernandez et al.
